definition: Adipose tissue is fat tissue, including white adipose tissue in the abdomen, made up of adipocytes that can become enlarged in obesity. In this packet, it is described as a biologically active tissue that releases adipokines, inflammatory mediators, and free fatty acids that may influence brain and blood-vessel function.

reasons: The definition states that adipose tissue includes “white adipose tissue in the abdomen,” but the packet discusses “visceral epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT)” in mice, not abdominal adipose tissue in general.

The definition claims adipocytes “can become enlarged in obesity,” but the packet only reports that lipectomy “reduced the number of severely hypertrophic adipocytes” in residual eWAT; it does not explicitly define adipocytes as enlarging in obesity in general terms.

The packet supports that adipose tissue is described as biologically active via secretion of adipokines/pro-inflammatory factors and that visceral WAT affects hippocampal (cerebrovascular) outcomes; however, those supported parts are mixed with the unsupported abdominal and general adipocyte-enlargement claims.
The requested field/sense is not defensible here: the packet is a biomedical article about adipose tissue, not a psychology/counselling sense of “learning.”

The definition adds location-specific detail (“white adipose tissue in the abdomen”) that is not stated in the packet; the packet discusses visceral epididymal white adipose tissue in mice, not abdominal adipose tissue generally.
The opening gloss “fat tissue” is too broad for the packet’s narrower focus on visceral white adipose tissue, and the definition blends in extra generalization beyond what is directly supported.
